A, smaller rate alone barely helps under unique decoding: each query buys at most one bit (distance below 1/2), so the query count floors near 130 while the codewords and Merkle paths keep growing. The best UDR rate, 1/8, gives 534 kB (−10 %) for +19 % prove.

B, Johnson over GF(2^256). Over GF(2^128), Johnson cannot reach 128 bits here. Round 0, the out-of-domain sample that pins the committed list element, is a polynomial of degree 2^22 − 1 in its challenge, and it keeps 97 bits (flock's own level-0 check stops at 118). With every Ligerito challenge in GF(2^256), Round 0 has 225 bits, fold grinding disappears, and queries fall with the rate: 244, 119, 79, 60 and 48 at the first level for rates 1/2 to 1/32 (UDR: 309 to 134). Extension messages take 32 bytes. At rate 1/2 alone: 512 kB (−14 %) for +8 % prove.

C, polylog bridge. The bridge used to send its 8,192 column sums (131 kB). Now the prover commits them, shifted by one so that no fold can alias 0 with 2^128 − 1 in the exponent. It then sends one root value, checked by a second product tree over the sums' bits, and proves the prime read-off with a small recursive bridge (16 sums in the clear). The sums are opened by their own Ligerito run at rate 1/32. The bridge falls from 145 to 75 kB; 46 kB of the 75 is that opening. Prove time changes by +7 to +37 ms and verify by +3 to 4 ms.

Together, Johnson at 1/8 with the polylog bridge gives 315 kB (−47 %) for +24 % prove. At 1/32 it gives 281 kB (−53 %) for +72 %, almost all of it commitment (76 → 490 ms). What remains at 1/32: PCS opening 133 kB, bridge 74 kB, and 66 kB of coefficient exception counts, two bytes per signature even when empty.

Caveats: the GF(2^256) profiles inherit 16-bit query grinding per level from flock's template (UDR has none; the per-site plan adds 4 bits). The extension opener is a direct implementation without the base opener's fused passes, so it costs about 60 ms more at the same rate. The polylog bridge opens its sums in a second Ligerito run rather than the single merged run of the polylog note. Two input seeds (42, 1), within 4 % of each other on every row.
